entries.f952a1dade042897d45ada32e1d2c74d739b4288: <div sID="gen1227" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="41" osisID="Gen.41" sID="Gen.41"/> <div eID="gen1227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1228" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1229" type="x-p"/> Two things Providence is here bringing about:—I. The advancement of Joseph. II. The maintenance of Jacob and his family in a time of famine; for the eyes of the Lord run to and fro through the earth, and direct the affairs of the children of men for the benefit of those few whose hearts are upright with him. In order to these, we have here, 1. Pharaoh's dreams, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.1-Gen.41.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. 2. The recommendation of Joseph to him for an interpreter, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.9-Gen.41.13">ver. 9-13</reference>. 3. The interpretation of the dreams, and the prediction of seven years of plenty and seven years of famine in Egypt, with the prudent advice given to Pharaoh thereupon, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.14-Gen.41.36">ver. 14-36</reference>. 4. The preferment of Joseph to a place of the highest power and trust in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.37-Gen.41.45">ver. 37-45</reference>. 5. The accomplishment of Joseph's prediction, and his fidelity to his trust, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.46-Gen.41.57">ver. 46</reference>, &c.
entries.291cb31083ed7cb50adbd93239c47d6a81c8519d: <div eID="gen1229" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1228" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Pharaoh's Portentous Dream. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1715.)</title> <div sID="gen1230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass at the end of two full years, that Pharaoh dreamed: and, behold, he stood by the river. 2 And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed; and they fed in a meadow. <hi type="super">3</hi> And, behold, seven other kine came up after them out of the river, ill favoured and leanfleshed; and stood by the <hi type="italic">other</hi> kine upon the brink of the river. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke. <hi type="super">5</hi> And he slept and dreamed the second time: and, behold, seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good. <hi type="super">6</hi> And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and, behold, <hi type="italic">it was</hi> a dream. <hi type="super">8</hi> And it came to pass in the morning that his spirit was troubled; and he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt, and all the wise men thereof: and Pharaoh told them his dreams; but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none that could interpret them unto Pharaoh. <div eID="gen1230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1231" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The delay of Joseph's enlargement. It was not till <hi type="italic">the end of two full years</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.1">v. 1</reference>); so long he waited after he had entrusted the chief butler with his case and began to have some prospect of relief. Note, We have need of patience, not only bearing, but waiting, patience. Joseph lay in prison until the time that his word came, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.19">Ps. cv. 19</reference>. There is a time set for the deliverance of God's people; that time will come, though it seem to tarry; and, when it comes, it will appear to have been the best time, and therefore we ought to wait for it (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab. ii. 3</reference>), and not think two full years too long to continue waiting. 2. The means of Joseph's enlargement, which were Pharaoh's dreams, here related. If we were to look upon them as ordinary dreams, we might observe from them the follies and absurdities of a roving working fancy, how it represents to itself tame cows as beasts of prey (nay, more ravenous than any, eating up those of their own kind), and ears of corn as devouring one another. Surely in the multitude of dreams, nay, even in one dream, there are divers vanities, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Eccl. v. 7</reference>. Now that God no longer speaks to us in that way, I think it is no matter how little we either heed them or tell them. Foolish dreams related can make no better than foolish talk. But these dreams which Pharaoh dreamed carried their own evidence with them that they were sent of God; and therefore, when he awoke, his spirit was troubled, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.8">v. 8</reference>. It cannot but put us into a concern to receive any extraordinary message from heaven, because we are conscious to ourselves that we have no reason to expect any good tidings thence. His magicians were puzzled, the rules of their art failed them: these dreams of Pharaoh, it seems, did not fall within the compass of them, so that they could not offer at the interpretation of them. This was to make Joseph's performance by the Spirit of God the more admirable. Human reason, prudence, and foresight, must be nonplussed, that divine revelation may appear the more glorious in the contrivance of our redemption, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.13-1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. 2. 13, 14</reference>. Compare with this story, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.27">Dan. ii. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.7">iv. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.8">v. 8</reference>. Joseph's own dreams were the occasion of his troubles, and now Pharaoh's dreams were the occasion of his enlargement.
entries.a1f864eb939740dcf61fcd8f2064a22fccb2b19d: <div eID="gen1231" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joseph Brought before Pharaoh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1715.)</title> <div sID="gen1232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Then spake the chief butler unto Pharaoh, saying, I do remember my faults this day: <hi type="super">10</hi> Pharaoh was wroth with his servants, and put me in ward in the captain of the guard's house, <hi type="italic">both</hi> me and the chief baker: <hi type="super">11</hi> And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he; we dreamed each man according to the interpretation of his dream. <hi type="super">12</hi> And <hi type="italic">there was</hi> there with us a young man, a Hebrew, servant to the captain of the guard; and we told him, and he interpreted to us our dreams; to each man according to his dream he did interpret. <hi type="super">13</hi> And it came to pass, as he interpreted to us, so it was; me he restored unto mine office, and him he hanged. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh. 15 And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I have dreamed a dream, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that can interpret it: and I have heard say of thee, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou canst understand a dream to interpret it. 16 And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. <div eID="gen1232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1233" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The recommending of Joseph to Pharaoh for an interpreter. The chief butler did it more in compliment to Pharaoh, to oblige him, than in gratitude to Joseph, or in compassion for his case. He makes a fair confession (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I remember my faults this day,</hi> in forgetting Joseph." Note, It is best to remember our duty, and to do it in its time; but, if we have neglected that, it is next best to remember our faults, and repent of them, and do our duty at last; better late than never. Some think he means his faults against Pharaoh, for which he was imprisoned; and then he would insinuate that, though Pharaoh had forgiven him, he had not forgiven himself. The story he had to tell was, in short, That there was an obscure young man in the king's prison, who had very properly interpreted his dream, and the chief baker's (the event corresponding in each with the interpretation), and that he would recommend him to the king his master for an interpreter. Note, God's time for the enlargement of his people will appear at last to be the fittest time. If the chief butler had at first used his interest for Joseph's enlargement, and had obtained it, it is probable that upon his release he would have gone back to <hi type="italic">the land of the Hebrews</hi> again, which he spoke of so feelingly (<reference osisRef="Gen.40.15">ch. xl. 15</reference>), and then he would neither have been so blessed himself, nor such a blessing to his family, as afterwards he proved. But staying two years longer, and coming out now upon this occasion, at last, to interpret the king's dreams, way was made for his very great preferment. Those that patiently wait for God shall be paid for their waiting, not only principal but interest, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">Lam. iii. 26</reference>. 2. The introducing of Joseph to Pharaoh. The king's business requires haste. Joseph is sent for out of the dungeon with all speed; Pharaoh's order discharged him both from his imprisonment and from his servitude, and made him a candidate for some of the highest trusts at court. The king can scarcely allow him time, but that decency required it, to shave himself, and to change his raiment, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.14">v. 14</reference>. It is done with all possible expedition, and Joseph is brought in, perhaps almost as much surprised as Peter was, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.9">Acts xii. 9</reference>. So suddenly is his captivity brought back that he is as one that dreams, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.1">Ps. cxxvi. 1</reference>. Pharaoh immediately, without enquiring who or whence he was, tells him his business, that he expected he should interpret his dream, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.15">v. 15</reference>. To which, Joseph makes him a very modest decent reply, (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.16">v. 16</reference>), in which, (1.) He gives honour to God. "It is not in me, God must give it." Note, Great gifts appear most graceful and illustrious when those that have them use them humbly, and take not the praise of them to themselves, but give it to God. To such God gives more grace. (2.) He shows respect to Pharaoh, and hearty good-will to him and his government, in supposing that the interpretation would be an answer of peace. Note, Those that consult God's oracles may expect an answer of peace. If Joseph be made the interpreter, hope the best.
entries.3ef18bb358816cfcdf8da4bb1ffeefb671553c53: <div eID="gen1233" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joseph Interprets Pharaoh's Dream. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1715.)</title> <div sID="gen1234" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, In my dream, behold, I stood upon the bank of the river: <hi type="super">18</hi> And, behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow: <hi type="super">19</hi> And, behold, seven other kine came up after them, poor and very ill favoured and leanfleshed, such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for badness: <hi type="super">20</hi> And the lean and the ill favoured kine did eat up the first seven fat kine: <hi type="super">21</hi> And when they had eaten them up, it could not be known that they had eaten them; but they <hi type="italic">were</hi> still ill favoured, as at the beginning. So I awoke. 22 And I saw in my dream, and, behold, seven ears came up in one stalk, full and good: <hi type="super">23</hi> And, behold, seven ears, withered, thin, <hi type="italic">and</hi> blasted with the east wind, sprung up after them: <hi type="super">24</hi> And the thin ears devoured the seven good ears: and I told <hi type="italic">this</hi> unto the magicians; but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none that could declare <hi type="italic">it</hi> to me. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Joseph said unto Pharaoh, The dream of Pharaoh <hi type="italic">is</hi> one: God hath showed Pharaoh what he <hi type="italic">is</hi> about to do. <hi type="super">26</hi> The seven good kine <hi type="italic">are</hi> seven years; and the seven good ears <hi type="italic">are</hi> seven years: the dream <hi type="italic">is</hi> one. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them <hi type="italic">are</hi> seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine. <hi type="super">28</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the thing which I have spoken unto Pharaoh: What God <hi type="italic">is</hi> about to do he showeth unto Pharaoh. <hi type="super">29</hi> Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt: <hi type="super">30</hi> And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine shall consume the land; <hi type="super">31</hi> And the plenty shall not be known in the land by reason of that famine following; for it <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> very grievous. <hi type="super">32</hi> And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; <hi type="italic">it is</hi> because the thing <hi type="italic">is</hi> established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass. <div eID="gen1234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1235" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Pharaoh relates his dream. He dreamt that he stood upon the bank of the river Nile, and saw the kine, both the fat ones and the lean ones, come out of the river. For the kingdom of Egypt had no rain, as appears, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.18">Zech. xiv. 18</reference>, but the plenty of the year depended upon the overflowing of the river, and it was about one certain time of the year that it overflowed. If it rose to fifteen or sixteen cubits, there was plenty; if to twelve or thirteen only, or under, there was scarcity. See how many ways Providence has of dispensing its gifts; yet, whatever the second causes are, our dependence is still the same upon the first Cause, who makes every creature that to us that it is, be it rain or river. <div eID="gen1235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1236" type="x-p"/> II. Joseph interprets his dream, and tells him that it signified seven years of plenty now immediately to ensue, which should be succeeded by as many years of famine. Observe, 1. The two dreams signified the same thing, but the repetition was to denote the certainty, the nearness, and the importance, of the event, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.32">v. 32</reference>. Thus God has often shown <hi type="italic">the immutability of his counsel by two immutable things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 17, 18</reference>. The covenant is sealed with two sacraments; and in the one of them there are both bread and wine, wherein the dream is one, and yet it is doubled, for the thing is certain. 2. Yet the two dreams had a distinct reference to the two things wherein we most experience plenty and scarcity, namely, grass and corn. The plenty and scarcity of grass for the cattle were signified by the fat kine and the lean ones; the plenty and scarcity of herb for the service of man by the full ears and the thin ones. 3. See what changes the comforts of this life are subject to. After great plenty may come great scarcity; how strong soever we may think our mountain stands, if God speak the word, it will soon be moved. We cannot be sure that <hi type="italic">to-morrow shall be as this day,</hi> next year as this, and <hi type="italic">much more abundant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Isa. lvi. 12</reference>. We must learn how to want, as well as how to abound. 4. See the goodness of God in sending the seven years of plenty before those of famine, that provision might be made accordingly. Thus he <hi type="italic">sets the one over-against the other,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccl. vii. 14</reference>. With what wonderful wisdom has Providence, that great housekeeper, ordered the affairs of this numerous family from the beginning hitherto! Great variety of seasons there have been, and the produce of the earth is sometimes more and sometimes less; yet, take one time with another, what was miraculous concerning the manna is ordinarily verified in the common course of Providence, <hi type="italic">He that gathers much has nothing over, and he that gathers little has no lack,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.16.18">Exod. xvi. 18</reference>. 5. See the perishing nature of our worldly enjoyments. The great increase of the years of plenty was quite lost and swallowed up in the years of famine; and the overplus of it, which seemed very much, yet did but just serve to keep men alive, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.29-Gen.41.31">v. 29-31</reference>. <hi type="italic">Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats, but God shall destroy both it and them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">1 Cor. vi. 13</reference>. There is bread which <hi type="italic">endures to everlasting life,</hi> which shall not be forgotten, and which it is worth while to labour for, <reference osisRef="John.6.27">John vi. 27</reference>. Those that make the things of this world their good things will find but little pleasure in remembering that they have received them, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>. 6. Observe, God revealed this beforehand to Pharaoh, who, as king of Egypt, was to be the father of his country, and to make prudent provision for them. Magistrates are called <hi type="italic">shepherds,</hi> whose care it must be, not only to rule, but to feed.
entries.20f952184bc650a27bfec35f80edd40c70c08147: <div eID="gen1236" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joseph's Exaltation. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1715.)</title> <div sID="gen1237" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man discreet and wise, and set him over the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">34</hi> Let Pharaoh do <hi type="italic">this,</hi> and let him appoint officers over the land, and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven plenteous years. <hi type="super">35</hi> And let them gather all the food of those good years that come, and lay up corn under the hand of Pharaoh, and let them keep food in the cities. <hi type="super">36</hi> And that food shall be for store to the land against the seven years of famine, which shall be in the land of Egypt; that the land perish not through the famine. <hi type="super">37</hi> And the thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Pharaoh said unto his servants, Can we find <hi type="italic">such a one</hi> as this <hi type="italic">is,</hi> a man in whom the Spirit of God <hi type="italic">is?</hi> <hi type="super">39</hi> And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, Forasmuch as God hath showed thee all this, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none so discreet and wise as thou <hi type="italic">art:</hi> <hi type="super">40</hi> Thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled: only in the throne will I be greater than thou. <hi type="super">41</hi> And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, See, I have set thee over all the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">42</hi> And Pharaoh took off his ring from his hand, and put it upon Joseph's hand, and arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck; <hi type="super">43</hi> And he made him to ride in the second chariot which he had; and they cried before him, Bow the knee: and he made him <hi type="italic">ruler</hi> over all the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">44</hi> And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> Pharaoh, and without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot in all the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">45</hi> And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnath-paaneah; and he gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On. And Joseph went out over <hi type="italic">all</hi> the land of Egypt. <div eID="gen1237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1238" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The good advice that Joseph gave to Pharaoh, which was, 1. That in the years of plenty he should lay up for the years of famine, buy up corn when it was cheap, that he might both enrich himself and supply the country when it would be dear and scarce. Note, Fair warning should always be followed with good counsel. Therefore the prudent man foresees the evil, that he may hide himself. God has in his word told us of a day of trial and exigence before us, when we shall need all the grace we can get, and all little enough, "Now, therefore, provide accordingly." Note, further, Times of gathering must be diligently improved, because there will come a time of spending. Let us go to the ant, and learn of her this wisdom, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6-Prov.6.8">Prov. vi. 6-8</reference>. 2. Because that which is everybody's work commonly proves nobody's work, he advises Pharaoh to appoint officers who should make it their business, and to select some one person to preside in the affair, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.33">v. 33</reference>. Probably, if Joseph had not advised this, it would not have been done; Pharaoh's counsellors could no more improve the dream than his magicians interpret it; therefore it is said of him (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.22">Ps. cv. 22</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">taught the senators, wisdom.</hi> Hence we may justly infer with Solomon (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13">Eccl. iv. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king.</hi> <div eID="gen1238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1239" type="x-p"/> II. The great honour that Pharaoh did to Joseph. 1. He gave him an honourable testimony: He is <hi type="italic">a man in whom the Spirit of God is;</hi> and this puts a great excellency upon any man; such men ought to be valued, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.38">v. 38</reference>. He is a nonsuch for prudence: <hi type="italic">There is none so discreet and wise as thou art,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.41.39">v. 39</reference>. Now he is abundantly recompensed for the disgrace that had been done him; and his righteousness is as the morning-light, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.6">Ps. xxxvii. 6</reference>. 2. He put him into an honourable office; not only employed him to buy up corn, but made him prime-minister of state, comptroller of the household—<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be over my house,</hi> chief justice of the kingdom—<hi type="italic">according to thy word shall all my people be ruled,</hi> or <hi type="italic">armed,</hi> as some read it, and then it bespeaks him general of the forces. Him commission was very ample: <hi type="italic">I have set thee over all the land of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.41">v. 41</reference>); <hi type="italic">without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.44">v. 44</reference>); all the affairs of the kingdom must pass through his hand. Nay (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.40">v. 40</reference>), <hi type="italic">only in the throne will I be greater than thou.</hi> Note, It is the wisdom of princes to prefer those, and the happiness of people to have those preferred, to places of power and trust, in whom the Spirit of God is. It is probable that there were those about the court who opposed Joseph's preferment, which occasioned Pharaoh so often to repeat the grant, and with that solemn sanction (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.44">v. 44</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am Pharaoh.</hi> When the proposal was made that there should be a corn-master-general nominated, it is said (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.37">v. 37</reference>), <hi type="italic">Pharaoh's servants were all pleased</hi> with the proposal, each hoping for the place; but when Pharaoh said to them, "Joseph shall be the man," we do not read that they made him any answer, being uneasy at it, and acquiescing only because they could not help it. Joseph had enemies, no doubt, archers that shot at him, and hated him (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.23">ch. xlix. 23</reference>), as Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.4">ch. vi. 4</reference>. 3. He put upon him all the marks of honour imaginable, to recommend him to the esteem and respect of the people as the king's favourite, and one whom he delighted to honour. (1.) He gave him his own ring, as a ratification of his commission, and in token of peculiar favour; or it was like delivering him the great seal. (2.) He put fine clothes upon him, instead of his prison garments. For those that are in kings' palaces must wear soft clothing; he that, in the morning, was dragging his fetters of iron, before night was adorned with a chain of gold. (3.) He made him <hi type="italic">ride in the second chariot</hi> to his own, and ordered all to do homage to him: "<hi type="italic">Bow the knee,</hi> as to Pharaoh himself." (4.) He gave him a new name, to show his authority over him, and yet such a name as bespoke the value he had for him, <hi type="italic">Zaphnath-paaneah—A revealer of secrets.</hi> (5.) He married him honourably to a prince's daughter. Where God had been liberal in giving wisdom and other merits, Pharaoh was not sparing in conferring honours. Now this preferment of Joseph was, [1.] An abundant recompense for his innocent and patient suffering, a lasting instance of the equity and goodness of Providence, and an encouragement to all good people to trust in a good God. [2.] It was typical of the exaltation of Christ, that great <hi type="italic">revealer of secrets</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">John i. 18</reference>), or, as some translate Joseph's new name, the <hi type="italic">Saviour of the world.</hi> The brightest glories of the upper world are put upon him, the highest trust is lodged in his hand, and all power is given to him both in heaven and earth. He is gatherer, keeper, and disposer, of all the stores of divine grace, and chief ruler of the kingdom of God among men. The work of ministers is to cry before him, "<hi type="italic">Bow the knee; kiss the Son.</hi>"
entries.a20d5aa0d7736c2d6057830925beffe110b7c0ad: <div eID="gen1239" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Famine in Egypt and Canaan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1706.)</title> <div sID="gen1240" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">46</hi> And Joseph <hi type="italic">was</hi> thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt. 47 And in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth by handfuls. <hi type="super">48</hi> And he gathered up all the food of the seven years, which were in the land of Egypt, and laid up the food in the cities: the food of the field, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> round about every city, laid he up in the same. <hi type="super">49</hi> And Joseph gathered corn as the sand of the sea, very much, until he left numbering; for <hi type="italic">it was</hi> without number. <hi type="super">50</hi> And unto Joseph were born two sons before the years of famine came, which Asenath the daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On bare unto him. <hi type="super">51</hi> And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, <hi type="italic">said he,</hi> hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. <hi type="super">52</hi> And the name of the second called he Ephraim: For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. <hi type="super">53</hi> And the seven years of plenteousness, that was in the land of Egypt, were ended. <hi type="super">54</hi> And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread. <hi type="super">55</hi> And when all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread: and Pharaoh said unto all the Egyptians, Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do. <hi type="super">56</hi> And the famine was over all the face of the earth: and Joseph opened all the storehouses, and sold unto the Egyptians; and the famine waxed sore in the land of Egypt. 57 And all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy <hi type="italic">corn;</hi> because that the famine was <hi type="italic">so</hi> sore in all lands. <div eID="gen1240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1241" type="x-p"/> Observe here, I. The building of Joseph's family in the birth of two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.50-Gen.41.52">v. 50-52</reference>. In the names he gave them, he owned the divine Providence giving this happy turn to his affairs, 1. He was made to forget his misery, <reference osisRef="Job.11.16">Job xi. 16</reference>. We should bear our afflictions when they are present as those that know not but Providence may so outweigh them by after-comforts as that we may even forget them when they are past. But could he be so unnatural as to <hi type="italic">forget all his father's house?</hi> He means the unkindness he received from his brethren, or perhaps the wealth and honour he expected from his father, with the birthright. The robes he now wore made him forget the coat of divers colours which he wore in his father's house. 2. He was made <hi type="italic">fruitful in the land of his affliction.</hi> It had been the land of his affliction, and in some sense it was still so, for it was not Canaan, the land of promise. His distance from his father was still his affliction. Note, Light is sometimes sown for the righteous in a barren and unlikely soil; and yet if God sow it, and water it, it will come up again. The afflictions of the saints promote their fruitfulness. <hi type="italic">Ephraim</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">fruitfulness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Manasseh forgetfulness,</hi> for these two often go together; when Jeshurun waxed fat, he forgot God his Maker. <div eID="gen1241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1242" type="x-p"/> II. The accomplishment of Joseph's predictions. Pharaoh had great confidence in the truth of them, perhaps finding in his own mind, beyond what another person could, an exact correspondence between them and his dreams, as between the key and the lock; and the event showed that he was not deceived. The seven plenteous years came (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.47">v. 47</reference>), and, at length, they were ended, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.54">v. 53</reference>. Note, We ought to foresee the approaching period of the days both of our prosperity and of our opportunity, and therefore must not be secure in the enjoyment of our prosperity nor slothful in the improvement of our opportunity; years of plenty will end, therefore, Whatever thy hand finds to do do it; and gather in gathering time. <hi type="italic">The morning cometh and also the night</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">Isa. xxi. 12</reference>), the plenty and also the famine. <hi type="italic">The seven years of dearth began to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.41.54">v. 54</reference>. See what changes of condition we are liable to in this world, and what need we have to be joyful in a day of prosperity and in a day of adversity to consider, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccl. vii. 14</reference>. This famine, it seems, was not only in Egypt, but in other lands, in <hi type="italic">all lands,</hi> that is, all the neighbouring countries; <hi type="italic">fruitful lands</hi> are soon <hi type="italic">turned into barrenness for the iniquity of those that dwell therein,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Ps. cvii. 34</reference>. It is here said that <hi type="italic">in the land of Egypt there was bread,</hi> meaning probably, not only that which Joseph had bought up for the king, but that which private persons, by his example, and upon the public notice of this prediction, as well as by the rules of common prudence, had laid up. <div eID="gen1242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1243" type="x-p"/> III. The performance of Joseph's trust. He was found faithful to it, as a steward ought to be. 1. He was diligent in laying up, while the plenty lasted, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.48-Gen.41.49">v. 48, 49</reference>. He that thus gathers is a wise son. 2. He was prudent and careful in giving out, when the famine came, and kept the markets low by furnishing them at reasonable rates out of his stores. The people in distress cried to Pharaoh, as that woman to the king of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.26">2 Kings vi. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">Help, my lord, O king:</hi> he sent them to his treasurer, <hi type="italic">Go to Joseph.</hi> Thus God in the gospel directs those that apply to him for mercy and grace to <hi type="italic">go to the Lord Jesus,</hi> in whom all fulness dwells; and, <hi type="italic">What he saith to you, do.</hi> Joseph, no doubt, with wisdom and justice fixed the price of the corn he sold, so that Pharaoh, whose money had bought it up, might have a reasonable profit, and yet the country might not be oppressed, nor advantage taken of their prevailing necessity; while he that withholdest corn when it is dear, in hopes it will yet grow dearer, though people perish for want of it, has many a curse for so doing (and it is not a curse causeless), <hi type="italic">blessings shall be upon the head of him that</hi> thus <hi type="italic">selleth it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.26">Prov. xi. 26</reference>. And let the price be determined by that golden rule of justice, to do as we would be done by.  <chapter eID="Gen.41"/> <div eID="gen1243" type="x-p"/>

entries.5a05c26ce622b01a04cb2c9f4c5f29a744e0696d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv461"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 41</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.41.1-Gen.41.24">Ge 41:1-24</reference>. Pharaoh's Dream.</title> <div sID="gen673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv461"/><hi type="bold">1. at the end of two full years--</hi>It is not certain whether these years are reckoned from the beginning of Joseph's imprisonment, or from the events described in the preceding chapter--most likely the latter. What a long time for Joseph to experience the sickness of hope deferred! But the time of his enlargement came when he had sufficiently learned the lessons of God designed for him; and the plans of Providence were matured.<div eID="gen673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pharaoh dreamed--</hi>"Pharaoh," from an Egyptian word Phre, signifying the "sun," was the official title of the kings of that country. The prince, who occupied the throne of Egypt, was Aphophis, one of the Memphite kings, whose capital was On or Heliopolis, and who is universally acknowledged to have been a patriot king. Between the arrival of Abraham and the appearance of Joseph in that country, somewhat more than two centuries had elapsed. Kings sleep and dream, as well as their subjects. And this Pharaoh had two dreams in one night so singular and so similar, so distinct and so apparently significant, so coherent and vividly impressed on his memory, that his spirit was troubled. <div eID="gen674" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8120383a0df6e28bbfb2a0972750a1b58a4f970: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv462"/><div sID="gen675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv462"/><hi type="bold">8. he called for all the magicians of Egypt--</hi>It is not possible to define the exact distinction between "magicians" and "wise men"; but they formed different branches of a numerous body, who laid claim to supernatural skill in occult arts and sciences, in revealing mysteries, explaining portents, and, above all, interpreting dreams. Long practice had rendered them expert in devising a plausible way of getting out of every difficulty and framing an answer suitable to the occasion. But the dreams of Pharaoh baffled their united skill. Unlike their Assyrian brethren (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.4">Da 2:4</reference>), they did not pretend to know the meaning of the symbols contained in them, and the providence of God had determined that they should all be nonplussed in the exercise of their boasted powers, in order that the inspired wisdom of Joseph might appear the more remarkable. <div eID="gen675" type="x-p"/>
entries.df592cf7bb0018f4190d5719c20e445ee1084d57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv463"/><div sID="gen676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv463"/><hi type="bold">9-13. then spake the chief butler unto Pharaoh, saying, I do remember my faults--</hi>This public acknowledgment of the merits of the young Hebrew would, tardy though it was, have reflected credit on the butler had it not been obviously made to ingratiate himself with his royal master. It is right to confess our faults against God, and against our fellow men when that confession is made in the spirit of godly sorrow and penitence. But this man was not much impressed with a sense of the fault he had committed against Joseph; he never thought of God, to whose goodness he was indebted for the prophetic announcement of his release, and in acknowledging his former fault against the king, he was practising the courtly art of pleasing his master. <div eID="gen676" type="x-p"/>
entries.63f89640ffa9a9162a53a07e314f432b11c84361: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv464"/><div sID="gen677" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv464"/><hi type="bold">14. Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph--</hi>Now that God's set time had come (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.19">Psa 105:19</reference>), no human power nor policy could detain Joseph in prison. During his protracted confinement, he might have often been distressed with perplexing doubts; but the mystery of Providence was about to be cleared up, and all his sorrows forgotten in the course of honor and public usefulness in which his services were to be employed.<div eID="gen677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shaved himself--</hi>The Egyptians were the only Oriental nation that liked a smooth chin. All slaves and foreigners who were reduced to that condition, were obliged, on their arrival in that country, to conform to the cleanly habits of the natives, by shaving their beards and heads, the latter of which were covered with a close cap. Thus prepared, Joseph was conducted to the palace, where the king seemed to have been anxiously waiting his arrival. <div eID="gen678" type="x-p"/>
entries.dff6f15264683694441e000f16d87b207f18fef8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv465"/><div sID="gen679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv465"/><hi type="bold">15-16. Pharaoh said, ... I have dreamed a dream--</hi>The king's brief statement of the service required brought out the genuine piety of Joseph; disclaiming all merit, he ascribed whatever gifts or sagacity he possessed to the divine source of all wisdom, and he declared his own inability to penetrate futurity; but, at the same time, he expressed his confident persuasion that God would reveal what was necessary to be known. <div eID="gen679" type="x-p"/>
entries.aec553f1f9d26dbc3a1ad87a65828121b738596b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv466"/><div sID="gen680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv466"/><hi type="bold">17. Pharaoh said, In my dream, behold, I stood upon the bank of the river--</hi>The dreams were purely Egyptian, founded on the productions of that country and the experience of a native. The fertility of Egypt being wholly dependent on the Nile, the scene is laid on the banks of that river; and oxen being in the ancient hieroglyphics symbolical of the earth and of food, animals of that species were introduced in the first dream. <div eID="gen680" type="x-p"/>
entries.3be55b26899715d0da40b2bb5d20d49134f7be0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv467"/><div sID="gen681" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv467"/><hi type="bold">18. there came up out of the river seven kine--</hi>Cows now, of the buffalo kind, are seen daily plunging into the Nile; when their huge form is gradually emerging, they seem as if rising "out of the river."<div eID="gen681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they fed in a meadow--</hi>Nile grass, the aquatic plants that grow on the marshy banks of that river, particularly the lotus kind, on which cattle were usually fattened. <div eID="gen682" type="x-p"/>
entries.592ad3014ce06a94b88aa0579723a2dc09f4f248: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv468"/><div sID="gen683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv468"/><hi type="bold">19. behold, seven other kine ... poor and ill-favoured--</hi>The cow being the emblem of fruitfulness, the different years of plenty and of famine were aptly represented by the different condition of those kine--the plenty, by the cattle feeding on the richest fodder; and the dearth, by the lean and famishing kine, which the pangs of hunger drove to act contrary to their nature. <div eID="gen683" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad5e06406144d16dd61fd54fc431ecf8da8208ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv469"/><div sID="gen684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv469"/><hi type="bold">22. I saw in my dream, and, behold, seven ears--</hi>that is, of Egyptian wheat, which, when "full and good," is remarkable in size (a single seed sprouting into seven, ten, or fourteen stalks) and each stalk bearing an ear. <div eID="gen684" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e490f88238878bb021fce1e690e7dc250d6aa4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv470"/><div sID="gen685" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv470"/><hi type="bold">23. blasted with the east wind--</hi>destructive everywhere to grain, but particularly so in Egypt; where, sweeping over the sandy deserts of Arabia, it comes in the character of a hot, blighting wind, that quickly withers all vegetation (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.12">Eze 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.15">Ho 13:15</reference>). <div eID="gen685" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7854a59b34484abca0e895eb4348b6eedb8fb41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv471"/><div sID="gen686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv471"/><hi type="bold">24. the thin ears devoured the seven good ears--</hi>devoured is a different word from that used in <reference osisRef="Gen.41.4">Ge 41:4</reference> and conveys the idea of destroying, by absorbing to themselves all the nutritious virtue of the soil around them. <div eID="gen686" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe4f3fe340497926ff5c261557fc8a52c11da5f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv472"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.41.25-Gen.41.36">Ge 41:25-36</reference>. Joseph Interprets Pharaoh's Dreams.</title> <div sID="gen687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv472"/><hi type="bold">25. Joseph said, ... The dream ... is one--</hi>They both pointed to the same event--a remarkable dispensation of seven years of unexampled abundance, to be followed by a similar period of unparalleled dearth. The repetition of the dream in two different forms was designed to show the absolute certainty and speedy arrival of this public crisis; the interpretation was accompanied by several suggestions of practical wisdom for meeting so great an emergency as was impending. <div eID="gen687" type="x-p"/>
entries.4219013f0dc111b44e564df3cace7074634cb968: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv473"/><div sID="gen688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv473"/><hi type="bold">33. Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man--</hi>The explanation given, when the key to the dreams was supplied, appears to have been satisfactory to the king and his courtiers; and we may suppose that much and anxious conversation arose, in the course of which Joseph might have been asked whether he had anything further to say. No doubt the providence of God provided the opportunity of his suggesting what was necessary. <div eID="gen688" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f166fe56e892822289eb5aeaaafb9f96255d00a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv474"/><div sID="gen689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv474"/><hi type="bold">34. and let him appoint officers over the land--</hi>overseers, equivalent to the beys of modern Egypt.<div eID="gen689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take up the fifth part of the land--</hi>that is, of the land's produce, to be purchased and stored by the government, instead of being sold to foreign corn merchants. <div eID="gen690" type="x-p"/>
entries.3136e07c233af89088bb1b3c02985ccee582f1a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv475"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.41.37-Gen.41.57">Ge 41:37-57</reference>. Joseph Made Ruler of Egypt.</title> <div sID="gen691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv475"/><hi type="bold">38. Pharaoh said unto his servants--</hi>The kings of ancient Egypt were assisted in the management of state affairs by the advice of the most distinguished members of the priestly order; and, accordingly, before admitting Joseph to the new and extraordinary office that was to be created, those ministers were consulted as to the expediency and propriety of the appointment.<div eID="gen691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man in whom the Spirit of God is--</hi>An acknowledgment of the being and power of the true God, though faint and feeble, continued to linger amongst the higher classes long after idolatry had come to prevail. <div eID="gen692" type="x-p"/>
entries.2aa1d67fd37944d530fe346b959e5a7f76500e54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv476"/><div sID="gen693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv476"/><hi type="bold">40. Thou shalt be over my house--</hi>This sudden change in the condition of a man who had just been taken out of prison could take place nowhere, except in Egypt. In ancient as well as modern times, slaves have often risen to be its rulers. But the special providence of God had determined to make Joseph governor of Egypt; and the way was paved for it by the deep and universal conviction produced in the minds both of the king and his councillors, that a divine spirit animated his mind and had given him such extraordinary knowledge.<div eID="gen693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled--</hi>literally, "kiss." This refers to the edict granting official power to Joseph, to be issued in the form of a firman, as in all Oriental countries; and all who should receive that order would kiss it, according to the usual Eastern mode of acknowledging obedience and respect for the sovereign [Wilkinson]. <div eID="gen694" type="x-p"/>
entries.78c37ac3386b2c8648ea909841949a94a6caa761: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv477"/><div sID="gen695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv477"/><hi type="bold">41. Pharaoh said, ... See, I have set thee over all the land--</hi>These words were preliminary to investiture with the insignia of office, which were these: the signet-ring, used for signing public documents, and its impression was more valid than the sign-manual of the king; the khelaat or dress of honor, a coat of finely wrought linen, or rather cotton, worn only by the highest personages; the gold necklace, a badge of rank, the plain or ornamental form of it indicating the degree of rank and dignity; the privilege of riding in a state carriage, the second chariot; and lastly-- <div eID="gen695" type="x-p"/>
entries.affae254de263156508077496469149cb1af7e8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv478"/><div sID="gen696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv478"/><hi type="bold">43. they cried before him, Bow the knee--</hi>abrech, an Egyptian term, not referring to prostration, but signifying, according to some, "father" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.45.8">Ge 45:8</reference>); according to others, "native prince"--that is, proclaimed him naturalized, in order to remove all popular dislike to him as a foreigner. <div eID="gen696" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4fcb7ebc1be49d2456929de0404a2586a83fdee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv479"/><div sID="gen697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv479"/>44. These ceremonies of investiture were closed in usual form by the king in council solemnly ratifying the appointment.<div eID="gen697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am Pharaoh, and without thee, &c.--</hi>a proverbial mode of expression for great power. <div eID="gen698" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bd726ca0dfd87b59fed89fce87f24c38d7b39bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv480"/><div sID="gen699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv480"/><hi type="bold">45. Zaphnath-paaneah--</hi>variously interpreted, "revealer of secrets"; "saviour of the land"; and from the hieroglyphics, "a wise man fleeing from pollution"--that is, adultery.<div eID="gen699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gave him to wife Asenath, the daughter of--</hi>His naturalization was completed by this alliance with a family of high distinction. On being founded by an Arab colony, Poti-pherah, like Jethro, priest of Midian, might be a worshipper of the true God; and thus Joseph, a pious man, will be freed from the charge of marrying an idolatress for worldly ends.<div eID="gen700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">On--</hi>called Aven (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.17">Eze 30:17</reference>) and also Beth-shemesh (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.13">Jr 43:13</reference>). In looking at this profusion of honors heaped suddenly upon Joseph, it cannot be doubted that he would humbly yet thankfully acknowledge the hand of a special Providence in conducting him through all his checkered course to almost royal power; and we, who know more than Joseph did, cannot only see that his advancement was subservient to the most important purposes relative to the Church of God, but learn the great lesson that a Providence directs the minutest events of human life. <div eID="gen701" type="x-p"/>
entries.17cf762cd1c62968e4e1581576af08ef66478e59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv481"/><div sID="gen702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv481"/><hi type="bold">46. Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh--</hi>seventeen when brought into Egypt, probably three in prison, and thirteen in the service of Potiphar.<div eID="gen702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went out ... all the land--</hi>made an immediate survey to determine the site and size of the storehouses required for the different quarters of the country. <div eID="gen703" type="x-p"/>
entries.413e7b5d2f270b5568c42d7cd1bb4a3afb6c6ccb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv482"/><div sID="gen704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv482"/><hi type="bold">47. the earth brought forth by handfuls--</hi>a singular expression, alluding not only to the luxuriance of the crop, but the practice of the reapers grasping the ears, which alone were cut. <div eID="gen704" type="x-p"/>
entries.7217ed36474a7e60063528c83be522732e4fe1f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv483"/><div sID="gen705" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv483"/><hi type="bold">48. he gathered up all the food of the seven years--</hi>It gives a striking idea of the exuberant fertility of this land, that, from the superabundance of the seven plenteous years, corn enough was laid up for the subsistence, not only of its home population, but of the neighboring countries, during the seven years of dearth. <div eID="gen705" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d275b33ab06969a26b8892a0bab0104f01ffd55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv484"/><div sID="gen706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv484"/><hi type="bold">50-52. unto Joseph were born two sons--</hi>These domestic events, which increased his temporal happiness, develop the piety of his character in the names conferred upon his children. <div eID="gen706" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce156e980b7211c133bf3eede6b8d81f006c9b5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv485"/><div sID="gen707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv485"/><hi type="bold">53-56. The seven years of plenteousness ... ended--</hi>Over and above the proportion purchased for the government during the years of plenty, the people could still have husbanded much for future use. But improvident as men commonly are in the time of prosperity, they found themselves in want, and would have starved by thousands had not Joseph anticipated and provided for the protracted calamity. <div eID="gen707" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4dfec3cb6dc9664480a0a676c9df5b9e76d3c78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv486"/><div sID="gen708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv486"/><hi type="bold">57. The famine was sore in all lands--</hi>that is, the lands contiguous to Egypt--Canaan, Syria, and Arabia. <chapter eID="Gen.41"/>

entries.1873d5a29220c1636a3ef365844cf41c47dffc16: <div eID="gen1865" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen1866" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1867" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1867" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1866" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1868" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh's dream of the seven well-favored and seven ill-favored kine, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.1-Gen.41.4">Gen 41:1-4</reference>. His dream of the seven full and seven thin ears of corn, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.5-Gen.41.7">Gen 41:5-7</reference>. The magicians and wise men applied to for the interpretation of them, but could give no solution, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.8">Gen 41:8</reference>. The chief butler recollects and recommends Joseph, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.9-Gen.41.13">Gen 41:9-13</reference>. Pharaoh commands him to be brought out of prison, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.14">Gen 41:14</reference>. Joseph appears before Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.15">Gen 41:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.16">Gen 41:16</reference>. Pharaoh repeats his dreams, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.17-Gen.41.24">Gen 41:17-24</reference>. Joseph interprets them, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.25-Gen.41.32">Gen 41:25-32</reference>, and gives Pharaoh directions how to provide against the approaching scarcity, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.33-Gen.41.36">Gen 41:33-36</reference>. Pharaoh, pleased with the counsel, appoints Joseph to be superintendent of all his affairs, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.37-Gen.41.41">Gen 41:37-41</reference>. Joseph receives the badges of his new office, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.42">Gen 41:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.43">Gen 41:43</reference>, and has his powers defined, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.44">Gen 41:44</reference>; receives a new name, and marries Asenath, daughter of Poti-Pherah, priest of On, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.45">Gen 41:45</reference>. Joseph's age when brought before Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.46">Gen 41:46</reference>. Great fertility of Egypt in the seven plenteous years, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.47">Gen 41:47</reference>. Joseph hoards up the grain, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.48">Gen 41:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.49">Gen 41:49</reference>. Ephraim and Manasseh born, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.50-Gen.41.52">Gen 41:50-52</reference>. The seven years of famine commence with great rigour, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.53-Gen.41.55">Gen 41:53-55</reference>. Joseph opens the storehouses to the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.56">Gen 41:56</reference>. People from the neighboring countries come to Egypt to buy corn, the famine being in all those lands, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.57">Gen 41:57</reference>. <div eID="gen1868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1869" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen1869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1870" type="x-p"/> Two full years - שנתים ימים shenathayim yamim, two years of days, two complete solar revolutions, after the events mentioned in the preceding chapter. <div eID="gen1870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1871" type="x-p"/> The river - The Nile, the cause of the fertility of Egypt.
entries.010e60fe965812be13829d33a3375057e46c39b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen1871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1872" type="x-p"/> There came up out of the river seven well-favored kine - This must certainly refer to the hippopotamus or river horse, as the circumstances of coming up out of the river and feeding in the field characterize that animal alone. The hippopotamus is the well-known inhabitant of the Nile, and frequently by night comes out of the river to feed in the fields, or in the sedge by the river side.
entries.22f6279148fdfa22858615274ff2f41f1960aa2f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen1872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1873" type="x-p"/> Blasted with the east wind - It has been very properly observed that all the mischief done to corn or fruit, by blasting, smutting, mildews, locusts, etc., is attributed to the east wind. See <reference osisRef="Exo.10.13">Exo 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.14.21">Exo 14:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.78.26">Psa 78:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.17.10">Eze 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jon.4.8">Jon 4:8</reference>. In Egypt it is peculiarly destructive, because it comes through the parched deserts of Arabia, often destroying vast numbers of men and women. The destructive nature of the simoom or smoom is mentioned by almost all travelers. Mr. Bruce speaks of it in his Travels in Egypt. On their way to Syene, Idris their guide, seeing one of these destroying blasts coming, cried out with a loud voice to the company, "Fall upon your faces, for here is the simoom! I saw," says Mr. B., "from the S. E. a haze come, in color like the purple part of the rainbow, but not so compressed or thick. It did not occupy twenty yards in breadth, and was about twelve feet high from the ground. It was a kind of blush upon the air, and it moved very rapidly, for I scarce could turn to fall upon the ground, with my head northward, when I felt the heat of its current plainly upon my face. We all lay flat upon the ground, as if dead, till Idris told us it was blown over. The meteor or purple haze which I saw was indeed passed, but the light air that still blew was of a heat to threaten suffocation. for my part, I found distinctly in my breast that I had imbibed a part of it; nor was I free from an asthmatic sensation till I had been some months in Italy, at the bathe of Poretta, near two years afterwards." - Travels, vol. vi., p. 462. On another occasion the whole company were made ill by one of these pestilential blasts, so that they had scarcely strength to load their camels - ibid., p. 484. The action of this destructive wind is referred to by the Prophet <reference osisRef="Hos.13.15">Hos 13:15</reference> : Though he be fruitful among his brethren, an East Wind shall come, the wind of the Lord shall come up From The Wilderness, and his spring shall Become Dry, and his fountain shall be Dried up: he shall spoil the treasure of all pleasant vessels.
entries.5da58375a24c239a0821cd1e448f566b0380458e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen1873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1874" type="x-p"/> Called for all the magicians - חרטמים chartummim. The word here used may probably mean no more than interpreters of abstruse and difficult subjects; and especially of the Egyptian hieroglyphics, an art which is now entirely lost. It is most likely that the term is Egyptian, and consequently its etymology must remain unknown to us. If Hebrew, Mr. Parkhurst's definition may be as good as any: "חרט cheret, a pen or instrument to write or draw with, and תם tam, to perfect or accomplish; those who were perfect in drawing their sacred, astrological, and hieroglyphical figures or characters, and who, by means of them, pretended to extraordinary feats, among which was the interpretation of dreams. They seem to have been such persons as Josephus (Ant., lib. ii., c. 9, s. 2) calls Ἱερογραμματεις sacred scribes, or professors of sacred learning." <div eID="gen1874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1875" type="x-p"/> Wise men - חכמיה chacameyha, the persons who, according to Porphyry, "addicted themselves to the worship of God and the study of wisdom, passing their whole life in the contemplation of Divine things. Contemplation of the stars, self-purification, arithmetic, and geometry, and singing hymns in honor of their gods, was their continual employment." - See Dodd. It was probably among these that Pythagoras conversed, and from whom he borrowed that modest name by which he wished his countrymen to distinguish him, viz., φιλοσοφος, a philosopher, simply, a lover of wisdom.
entries.a6241bb93ca3fb8303299c271116371dd7f25311: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen1875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1876" type="x-p"/> I do remember my faults - It is not possible he could have forgotten the circumstance to which he here alludes; it was too intimately connected with all that was dear to him, to permit him ever to forget it. But it was not convenient for him to remember this before; and probably he would not have remembered it now, had he not seen, that giving this information in such a case was likely to serve his own interest. We are justified in thinking evil of this man because of his scandalous neglect of a person who foretold the rescue of his life from imminent destruction, and who, being unjustly confined, prayed to have his case fairly represented to the king that justice might be done him; but this courtier, though then in the same circumstances himself, found it convenient to forget the poor, friendless Hebrew slave!
entries.c16fa96623d1ca306d51cc243ea646298d6837d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen1876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1877" type="x-p"/> They brought him hastily out of the dungeon - Pharaoh was in perplexity on account of his dreams; and when he heard of Joseph, he sent immediately to get him brought before him. He shaved himself - having let his beard grow all the time he was in prison, he now trimmed it, for it is not likely that either the Egyptians or Hebrews shaved themselves in our sense of the word: the change of raiment was, no doubt, furnished out of the king's wardrobe; as Joseph, in his present circumstances, could not be supposed to have any changes of raiment.
entries.59545e76a8ad588bba4169f66f46979f0820320f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen1877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1878" type="x-p"/> It is not in me, etc. - בלעדי biladai, without or independently of me - I am not essential to thy comfort, God himself has thee under his care. And he will send thee, or answer thee, peace; thou shalt have prosperity (שלום shelom) howsoever ominous thy dreams may appear. By this answer he not only conciliated the mind of the king, but led him to expect his help from that God from whom alone all comfort, protection, and prosperity, must proceed.
entries.7d214329e91a83459b2bc2d94168e63cc92e6e0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen1878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1879" type="x-p"/> Seven kine, fat-fleshed - See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.2">Gen 41:2</reference> (note). And observe farther, that the seven fat and the seven lean kine coming out of the same river plainly show, at once, the cause both of the plenty and the dearth. It is well known that there is scarcely any rain in Egypt; and that the country depends for its fertility on the overflowing of the Nile; and that the fertility is in proportion to the duration and quantity of the overflow. We may therefore safely conclude that the seven years of plenty were owing to an extraordinary overflowing of the Nile; and that the seven years of dearth were occasioned by a very partial, or total want of this essentially necessary inundation. Thus then the two sorts of cattle, signifying years of plenty and want, might be said to come out of the same river, as the inundation was either complete, partial, or wholly restrained. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.31">Gen 41:31</reference> (note).
entries.94e6af7b48c680e144a60d7ea7d65368f00af0a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen1879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1880" type="x-p"/> And when they had eaten them up, etc. - Nothing can more powerfully mark the excess and severity of the famine than creatures of the beeve or of the hippopotamus kind eating each other, and yet without any effect; remaining as lean and as wretched as they were before. A sense of want increases the appetite, and stimulates the digestive powers to unusual action; hence the concoction of the food becomes very rapid, and it is hurried through the intestines before its nutritive particles can be sufficiently absorbed; and thus, though much is eaten, very little nourishment is derived from it. And when they had eaten them up, it could not be known that they had eaten them; but they were still ill favored, as at the beginning. A most nervous and physically correct description.
entries.025e94b126af790d08d013fcee1e1537329790bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen1880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1881" type="x-p"/> God hath showed Pharaoh what he is about to do - Joseph thus shows the Egyptian king that though the ordinary cause of plenty or want is the river Nile, yet its inundations are under the direction of God: the dreams are sent by him, not only to signify beforehand the plenty and want, but to show also that all these circumstances, however fortuitous they may appear to man, are under the direction of an overruling Providence.
entries.1816e397d0e70829caa30f5472fafaa7ad3f09e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen1881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1882" type="x-p"/> The plenty shall not be known in the land by reason of that famine following - As Egypt depends for its fertility on the flowing of the Nile, and this flowing is not always equal, there must be a point to which it must rise to saturate the land sufficiently, in order to produce grain sufficient for the support of its inhabitants. Pliny, Hist. Nat., lib. v., cap. 9, has given us a scale by which the plenty and dearth may be ascertained; and, from what I have been able to collect from modern travelers, this scale may be yet considered as perfectly correct. <div eID="gen1882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1883" type="x-p"/> Justum incrementum est cubitorum 16. Minores aquae non omnia rigant, ampliores detinent, tardius recedendo. Hae serendi tempora absumunt, solo madente, Illae non dant, sitiente. Utrumque reputat provincia. In 12. cubitis famen sentit. In 13. etiamnum esurit; 14. cubita hilaritatem afferunt; 15. securitatem; 16. delicias. "The ordinary height of the inundations is sixteen cubits. When the waters are lower than this standard they do not overflow the whole ground; when above this standard, they are too long in running off. In the first case the ground is not saturated: by the second, the waters are detained so long on the ground that seed-time is lost. The province marks both. If it rise only twelve cubits, a famine is the consequence. Even at thirteen cubits hunger prevails; fourteen cubits produces general rejoicing; fifteen, perfect security; and sixteen, all the luxuries of life." <div eID="gen1883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1884" type="x-p"/> When the Nile rises to eighteen cubits it prevents the sowing of the land in due season, and as necessarily produces a famine as when it does not overflow its banks.
entries.0c84ce21e430255eea0fefdf654ecc33b71883dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen1884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1885" type="x-p"/> A man discreet and wise - As it is impossible that Joseph could have foreseen his own elevation, consequently he gave this advice without any reference to himself. The counsel therefore was either immediately inspired by God, or was dictated by policy, prudence, and sound sense.
entries.20ea1ac9eb06b246ea1a1190a0c8170c3dfc78d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen1885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1886" type="x-p"/> Let him appoint officers - פקדים pekidim, visitors, overseers: translated by Ainsworth, bishops; see <reference osisRef="Gen.39.1">Gen 39:1</reference>. <div eID="gen1886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1887" type="x-p"/> Take up the fifth part of the land - What is still called the meery, or that part of the produce which is claimed by the king by way of tax. It is probable that in Joseph's time it was not so much as a fifth part, most likely a tenth: but as this was an extraordinary occasion, and the earth brought forth by handfuls, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.47">Gen 41:47</reference>, the king would be justified in requiring a fifth; and from the great abundance, the people could pay this increased tax without feeling it to be oppressive.
entries.66c6780c8fa652409a9697962d79638c249c9f88: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen1887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1888" type="x-p"/> Under the hand of Pharaoh - To be completely at the disposal of the king.
entries.8aa716414f447b43eaa3ba0fec7ea78ef68be3c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen1888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1889" type="x-p"/> The thing was good - Pharaoh and his courtiers saw that the counsel was prudent, and should be carefully followed.
entries.4ea345e3dc9e1820a921f1ac0a7dd7beab74ccaf: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen1889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1890" type="x-p"/> In whom the Spirit of God is? - רוח אלהים ruach Elohim, the identical words used <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen 1:2</reference>; and certainly to be understood here as in the preceding place. If the Egyptians were idolaters, they acknowledged Joseph's God; and it is not to be supposed that they only became acquainted with him on this occasion. The knowledge of the true God was in Egypt long before; but it is very likely that though they acknowledged his influence with respect to Joseph, as they saw most clearly that he acted under an influence far beyond that of their magicians, for he interpreted dreams which they could not; yet they might, notwithstanding, have their gods many and their lords many at this time, for we know that in religious matters they were exceedingly corrupt afterwards.
entries.9251277acbc76b3da9941907fbb83ba5ee73c2b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen1890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1891" type="x-p"/> According unto thy word shall all my people be ruled - Literally, At thy mouth shall all my people kiss. In the eastern countries it is customary to kiss any thing that comes from a superior, and this is done by way of testifying respect and submission. In this sense the words in the text are to be understood: All the people shall pay the profoundest respect and obedience to all thy orders and commands. <div eID="gen1891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1892" type="x-p"/> Only in the throne will I be greater than thou - This, in one word, is a perfect description of a prime minister. Thou shalt have the sole management, under me, of all state affairs.
entries.17e8b41fef12cb97111899da0ea657cbc93af7d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen1892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1893" type="x-p"/> And Pharaoh took off his ring - and put it upon Joseph's hand - In this ring was probably set the king's signet, by which the royal instruments were sealed; and thus Joseph was constituted what we would call Lord Chancellor, or Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal. <div eID="gen1893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1894" type="x-p"/> Vestures of fine linen - שש shesh. Whether this means linen or cotton is not known. It seems to have been a term by which both were denominated; or it may be some other substance or cloth with which we are unacquainted. If the fine linen of Egypt was such as that which invests the bodies of the mummies, and these in general were persons of the first distinction, and consequently were enveloped in cloth of the finest quality, it was only fine comparatively speaking, Egypt being the only place at that time where such cloth was manufactured. I have often examined the cloth about the bodies of the most splendidly ornamented mummies, and found it sackcloth when compared with the fine Irish linens. As this shesh appears to have been a part of the royal clothing, it was probably both scarce and costly. "By comparing," says Parkhurst, "<reference osisRef="Exo.25.4">Exo 25:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.26.1">Exo 26:1</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.14">2Chr 2:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exo.26.31">Exo 26:31</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.14">2Chr 3:14</reference>, it appears that בוץ buts, cotton, is called שש shesh; and by comparing <reference osisRef="Exo.28.42">Exo 28:42</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Exo.39.28">Exo 39:28</reference>, that בד bad, linen, is also called שש shesh; so that shesh seems a name expressive of either of these, from their cheerful vivid whiteness." <div eID="gen1894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1895" type="x-p"/> Put a gold chain about his neck - This was not merely a badge of office. The chain might be intended to point out the union which should subsist between all parts of the government - the king, his ministers, and the people; as also that necessary dependence which they had reciprocally on each other, as well as the connection which must be preserved between the different members of the body politic, and the laws and institutions by which they were to be governed. Its being of gold might be intended to show the excellence, utility, and permanence of a government constituted on wise, just, and equal laws. We are justified in drawing such inferences as these, because in ancient times, in all nations, every thing was made an emblem or representation of some spiritual or moral subject it is strange that, probably without adverting to the reasons, the chain of gold worn about the neck is in different nations an emblem of civil authority.
entries.b4fbd640616f68153a5460df4e7b97b9471b71f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen1895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1896" type="x-p"/> He made him to ride in the second chariot - That which usually followed the king's chariot in public ceremonies. <div eID="gen1896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1897" type="x-p"/> Bow the knee - אברך abrech, which we translate bow the knee, and which we might as well translate any thing else, is probably an Egyptian word, the signification of which is utterly unknown. If we could suppose it to be a Hebrew word, it might be considered as compounded of אב ab, father, and רך rach, tender; for Joseph might be denominated a father, because of his care over the people, and the provision he was making for their preservation; and tender because of his youth. Or it may be compounded of אב ab, father, and ברך barech, blessing, the latter ב beth being easily lost in the preceding one; and Joseph might have this epithet as well as the other, on account of the care he was taking to turn aside the heavy curse of the seven years of famine, by accumulating the blessings of the seven years of plenty. Besides, father seems to have been a name of office, and probably father of the king or father of Pharaoh might signify the same as the king's minister among us; see on <reference osisRef="Gen.45.8">Gen 45:8</reference> (note). But if it be an Egyptian word, it is vain to look for its signification in Hebrew.
entries.ba94c9ec074db358a94ae9c37ea5185d29f7b204: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen1897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1898" type="x-p"/> I am Pharaoh - The same as if he had said, I am the king; for Pharaoh was the common title of the sovereigns of Egypt.
entries.948a961f2a6836c107ec1834bb62d945265e527e: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen1898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1899" type="x-p"/> Zaphnath-paaneah - The meaning of this title is as little known as that of abrech in the preceding verse. Some translate it, The revealer of secrets; others, The treasury of glorious comfort. St. Jerome translates the whole verse in the most arbitrary manner. Vertitque nomen ejus, et vocavit eum, lingua Aegyptiaca, Salvatorem mundi. "And he changed his name, and called him in the Egyptian language, The savior of the world." None of the Asiatic versions acknowledge this extraordinary gloss, and it is certainly worthy of no regard. The Anglo-Saxon nearly copies the Vulgate: And named him in Egyptian, The healer of the world. All the etymologies hitherto given of this word are, to say the least of them, doubtful. I believe it also to be an Egyptian epithet, designating the office to which he was now raised; and similar to our compound terms, Prime-Minister, Lord Chancellor, High-Treasurer, Chief Justice, etc. <div eID="gen1899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1900" type="x-p"/> Asenath the daughter of Poti-pherah - There is no likelihood that the Poti-pherah mentioned here is the same as the Potiphar who had purchased Joseph, and, on the false accusations of his wife, cast him into prison. 1. The Scripture gives no intimation that they were one and the same person. 2. Poti-pherah had children, and Potiphar was an eunuch; See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.37.36">Gen 37:36</reference> (note); for though eunuchs often kept women, there is no proof that they had any issue by them. <div eID="gen1900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1901" type="x-p"/> Priest of On - For the signification of the word כהן cohen or priest, See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Gen 14:18</reference> (note). On is rendered Heliopolis (the city of the sun) by the Septuagint and Anglo-Saxon; and it is very likely that this Poti-pherah was intendant of that nome or province, under Pharaoh. <div eID="gen1901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1902" type="x-p"/> Joseph went out over all the land - No doubt for the building of granaries, and appointing proper officers to receive the corn in every place, as Dr. Dodd has very properly conjectured.
entries.98b2a6a87513da18792311f24a6baf28870f623b: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen1902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1903" type="x-p"/> Joseph was thirty years old - As he was seventeen years old when he was sold into Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.2">Gen 37:2</reference>, and was now thirty, he must have been thirteen years in slavery. <div eID="gen1903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1904" type="x-p"/> Stood before Pharaoh - This phrase always means admission to the immediate presence of the sovereign, and having the honor of his most unlimited confidence. Among the Asiatic princes, the privilege of coming even to their seat, of standing before them, etc., was granted only to the highest favorites.
entries.bb0ed3bedea9c051dcf6381ec1c3fa42bd73651b: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen1904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1905" type="x-p"/> The earth brought forth by handfuls - This probably refers principally to rice, as it grows in tufts, a great number of stalks proceeding from the same seed.
