                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XLI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND it came to pass at the end of two <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> year of days.</ns0:note> full years <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">After the Butlers restitution to his place. Heb. <ns0:hi>years of days,</ns0:hi> for full years, as 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 14. 28. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 28. 3. as <ns0:hi>a month of days</ns0:hi> is put for a full month, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 29. 14. which is compleat to a day.</ns0:note>, that Pharaoh dreamed: and behold, he stood by the river <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Nilus,</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>the River</ns0:hi> simply, because of its emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nency, as <ns0:hi>Homer</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Virgil</ns0:hi> are called, <ns0:hi>the Poet.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And behold, there came up out of the ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This suits well with the nature of the thing, for both the fruitfulness and the barrenness of <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> depended under God upon the increase or diminution of the waters of that River.</ns0:note>, seven well-favoured kine <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Which when they appeared in dreams did portend, in the opinion of the learned <ns0:hi>Egyptians,</ns0:hi> the years or times to come, and them either good or bad according to their quality.</ns0:note>, and fat-fleshed, and they fed in a medow.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And behold, seven other kine came up after them out of the river, ill-favoured, and lean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fleshed, and stood by the <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> kine upon the brink of the river <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which shews how sparingly the river overflowed the Lands.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And the ill-favoured and lean-fleshed kine, did eat up the seven well-favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And he slept, and dreamed the second time: and behold, seven ears of corn <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which are fit and proper resemblances of the thing here intended, both because the fertility of a Land doth mainly con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sist in the abundance and goodness of these, and because, <ns0:hi>ears of Corn</ns0:hi> appearing to any in a dream did, in the judgment of the <ns0:hi>Egyptian</ns0:hi> wise-men, signifie years, as <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> notes.</ns0:note> came up upon one stalk, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>at.</ns0:note> rank and good.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the East-wind <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">A boisterous wind, and in those parts of the World very pernicious to the fruits of the Earth, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 17. 10. and 19. 12. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 13. 15.</ns0:note>, sprang up after them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears: and Pharaoh awoke, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold it was a dream <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Not a realthing, as <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> in his sleep imagined it to be. Heb. <ns0:hi>behold the dream.</ns0:hi> i. e. The dream did not vanish, as dreams commonly do, but was fixed in his mind, and he could not shake it off: by which he saw that it was no common or natu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral, but a divine and significant, dream.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And it came to pass in the morning, that his spirit was troubled <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Because he understood not the meaning of it, and dreaded the consequences of it. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 40. 6. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2. 1, 3. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27. 19.</ns0:note>, and he sent and called for all the Magicians <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whose profession it was to discover secret and future things, which they did either by the observation of the Stars, or by other superstitious practises and the help of evil spirits. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 7. 11, and 8. 19. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2. 2, 10.</ns0:note> of Egypt, and all the wise men <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Who were conversant in the study of nature, and by reason of their great sagacity did oft-times make happy conjectures.</ns0:note> thereof; and Pharaoh told them his dream <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">He calls them both one dream, either because they seemed to portend the same thing, or because they were the product of one night and were divided onely by a very little interruption.</ns0:note>: but there was none that could interpret them unto Pharaoh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Then spake the chief Butler unto Pharaoh, saying, I do remember my faults <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not against <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> by ingratitude, but against the King: by which expression he both acknowledgeth the Kings justice in imprisoning him and his clemency in pardoning him.</ns0:note> this day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Pharaoh was wroth with his servants, and put me in ward in the captain of the guards house, <ns0:hi>both</ns0:hi> me, and the chief baker.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he: we dreamed each man according to the inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pretation of his dream <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">Of which phrase see on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 40. 5.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> there with us a young man, an Hebrew, servant to the captain of the guard: and we told him, and he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 40. 12. &c.</ns0:note> interpreted to us our dreams, to each man according to his dream, he did interpret.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And it came to pass, as he interpreted to us, so it was, me he <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Either 1. <ns0:hi>Pharaoh.</ns0:hi> But then he would have mentioned either his name or title, and not have spoken so slightly and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />decently of him. Or rather 2. <ns0:hi>Ioseph,</ns0:hi> of whom he spake last, and who is here said to restore the one, and to hang the other, because he foretold those events, as <ns0:hi>Ieremy</ns0:hi> is said to <ns0:hi>pull down and destroy</ns0:hi> those Nations, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 1. 10. whose destruction he did onely foretell.</ns0:note> restored unto mine office, and him he hanged.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 105. 20</ns0:note> The Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> made him run.</ns0:note> brought him hastily out of the dunge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Prison,</ns0:hi> by a Synecdoche of the part for the whole. For it is not probable that <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> who was now so much employed and entrusted with all the affairs of the prison and Prisoners, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 39. 21, 22, 23. should still be kept in the dungeon properly so called.</ns0:note>: and he shaved himself <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">For till then he suffered his hair to grow, as the manner was for persons in prison or under great sorrow, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 24. But to appear in a mournful dress before the King was not convenient, nor usual. Compare <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 4. 4.</ns0:note>, and changed his rai<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, and came in unto Pharaoh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I have dream<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed a dream, and there is none that can interpret it: and I have heard say of thee, that <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, when <ns0:hi>th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>s hearest a dream, thou canst inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pret it.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> thou canst understand a dream, to interpret it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, it is not in me <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">I cannot do this by any power or vertue or art of my own, for I am but a man, as your Magicians are, but onely by inspiration from the great God. Thus he gives the honour from himself unto God, and leads <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> to the knowledge of the true God. For the phrase compare <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10. 20. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15. 10.</ns0:note>: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>May God give,</ns0:hi> &c. It is my desire that God would vouchsa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e to <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> a comfortable and happy an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swer.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:39" />17 And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, In my dream, behold, I stood upon the bank of a River.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fat-fleshed, and well-favoured, and they sed in a medow.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And behold, seven other kine came up af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter them, poor and very ill-favoured, and lean-flesh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for badness.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And the lean, and the ill-favoured kine, did eat up the first seven fat kine.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And when they had <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> come to the inward parts of them.</ns0:note> eaten them up, it could not be known that they had eaten them <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">They seemed to be neither fatter in the flesh, nor fuller in their bodies. As many times in Famine men eat much, but are not satisfied, because God withdraws his blessing from it, by which alone it is that meat nourisheth us.</ns0:note>, but they were still ill-favoured, as at the begin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning: So I awoke.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And I saw in my dream, and behold, seven ears came up in one stalk, full and good.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And behold, seven ears <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> small.</ns0:note> withered, thin, and blasted with the East-wind, sprung up after them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And the thin ears devoured the seven good ears: and I told this unto the Magicians, but there was none that could declare <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> to me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And Joseph said unto Pharaoh, The dream of Pharaoh is one <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To wit, In its design and signification, both dreams por<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tend the same thing.</ns0:note>, God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 The seven good kine are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years: the dream is one.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And the seven thin and ill-favoured kine that came up after them, are seven years: and the seven empty ears blasted with the East-wind, shall be seven years of famine.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the thing which I have spoken unto Pharaoh: what God is about to do, he sheweth unto Pharaoh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Behold, there come seven years of great plenty, throughout all the land of Egypt.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And there shall arise after them seven years of famine, and all the plenty shall be forgotten <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">There shall be no relicks of it to keep it in mens minds, which will be so taken up with the contemplation of their pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent misery and future danger, that they will have neither heart nor leasure to reflect upon their former plenty, the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />membrance whereof will but aggravate the present calamity.</ns0:note> in the land of Egypt: and the famine shall consume the land.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And the plenty shall not be known in the land, by reason of that famine following: for it <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> very <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> heavy.</ns0:note> grievous.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> because the thing is <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> prepared of God.</ns0:note> esta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blished by God: and God will shortly bring it to pass.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man discreet and wise, and set him over the land of Egypt.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 Let Pharaoh do <ns0:hi>this,</ns0:hi> and let him appoint <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> overseers.</ns0:note> officers over the land, and take up <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Not by force or violence, for <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> would never be the author of such unrighteous Counsels, but by purchase at the common price, which was like to be very low in that case, and therefore might easily be compassed by that rich and mighty Prince.</ns0:note> the fifth part <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Why not half, seeing the years of Famine were as many as the years of plenty? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Because 1. Men would and should live more sparingly in times of Famine. 2. It was likely that very many men would lay up great quantities of Corn in those years, partly because they could not spend it all, and partly in expectation of a scarcer and dearer time, when they might either use it themselves or <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
